name: Patellofemoral pain
definition: Pain around or behind the kneecap, brought on by activities that load the knee while it is bent.

typicalPopulation.text: Common in adolescents and young adults
Often active, but happens in non-athletes too

typicalPopulation.detail: The size of this difference varies between studies and the reasons are not settled. It is a weak prior, not a diagnostic feature.

zones.label: Around the kneecap
zones.note: Usually diffuse — patients circle the area rather than point to it.

zones.label: Behind the kneecap
zones.note: Often described as deep or hard to reach.

zones.label: Inferior pole of patella
zones.note: Pinpoint pain here fits patellar tendinopathy better.

zones.label: Medial or lateral joint line
zones.note: Joint line pain points away from patellofemoral pain.

symptoms.text: Pain with squatting, stairs, or running
symptoms.detail: These share one feature: they load the knee in flexion, which raises patellofemoral joint stress.

symptoms.text: Pain after sitting for a long time
symptoms.detail: Sometimes called the theatre sign. Sustained flexion without movement is the provocation.

symptoms.text: Follows a change in activity or training load
Grinding or clicking may be present
symptoms.detail: Crepitus is common in painless knees too. It does not indicate damage and should not be presented to patients as though it does.

signs.text: Familiar pain reproduced by a loaded knee task
Reduced control during single-leg tasks may be seen
signs.detail: Dynamic valgus and pelvic drop are frequently observed, but they also occur in people without pain. Treat as a treatment target, not a diagnostic criterion.

keyQuestions.text: What has changed in your activity recently?
Can you point to exactly where it hurts?
Does it hurt after sitting for a while?
Does it ever lock or give way?
keyQuestions.detail: Screens for mechanical symptoms. True locking points elsewhere; pseudo-giving-way from pain inhibition is common here.

expected.text: Familiar pain during a squat or step-down

supportive.detail: Informs treatment rather than diagnosis. Deficits are common but not required for the diagnosis.

supportive.text: Record a functional task you can retest

doesNotFit.detail: Patellofemoral pain does not usually swell. An effusion moves you toward intra-articular pathology or inflammatory arthropathy.

doesNotFit.text: Significant trauma, or inability to weight-bear
doesNotFit.detail: Apply the Ottawa Knee Rule to decide on radiography.

redFlags.detail: Septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Same-day medical referral.

redFlags.text: Pain progressing into walking or rest
redFlags.detail: Raises bone stress injury, particularly with a training spike or menstrual dysfunction. Stop loading and investigate.

redFlags.text: Adolescent with knee pain and a limp
redFlags.detail: Always examine the hip. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis can present as knee pain.

managementPrinciples.text: Explain it is load-related and usually settles
Adjust load rather than stopping activity
Retest the functional task to show progress
Set expectations: improvement takes weeks, not days
managementPrinciples.detail: Slower recovery is common, and a proportion of patients report symptoms years later. Saying so early protects the therapeutic relationship.

takeaways: Diffuse pain around or behind the kneecap.
Worse with squatting, stairs, and prolonged sitting.
Usually follows a change in load.
No single special test confirms it.
Swelling or true locking means think again.

location.prompt: Tap where this pain is most commonly reported.
location.feedbackCorrect: That's the typical area — diffuse, around or behind the kneecap.
location.feedbackIncorrect: Not typical. Patellofemoral pain sits around or behind the kneecap, and patients usually circle it rather than point.

presentation.feedbackCorrect: Good — loaded flexion and gradual onset are the pattern.
presentation.feedbackIncorrect: Locking and effusion point away from patellofemoral pain.

differentials.prompt: Which finding makes patellar tendinopathy more likely?

options.text: Pinpoint tenderness at the inferior pole

differentials.feedbackCorrect: Yes — tendinopathy is focally tender, patellofemoral pain is not.
differentials.feedbackIncorrect: Those two describe patellofemoral pain. Tendinopathy is pinpoint at the inferior pole.

safety.prompt: A 13-year-old has anterior knee pain and walks with a limp. What now?

options.text: Examine the hip before treating the knee
Reassure and review in six weeks

safety.feedbackCorrect: Correct — hip pathology refers to the knee in this age group.
safety.feedbackIncorrect: In an adolescent with a limp, the hip must be examined first. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis presents as knee pain.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where is the pain usually felt?
options: Diffusely around or behind the kneecap
Pinpoint at the inferior pole of the patella
knowledgeCheck.feedback: Patients typically circle the area rather than point to one spot.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which activity is most characteristic?
knowledgeCheck.feedback: Loaded knee flexion is the provocation. Descending stairs loads it most.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which finding argues AGAINST patellofemoral pain?
knowledgeCheck.feedback: Patellofemoral pain does not usually swell. An effusion means reconsider.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which test confirms the diagnosis?
knowledgeCheck.feedback: It is a clinical diagnosis based on reproducing familiar pain with loaded flexion, after excluding other causes.

knowledgeCheck.question: A 13-year-old has anterior knee pain and a limp. What must you do?
knowledgeCheck.feedback: Hip pathology refers to the knee. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is the one you cannot miss.

diagnosticCriteria: Retropatellar or peri-patellar pain reproduced by activities that load the flexed knee.
Other sources of anterior knee pain excluded on history and examination.
deepDive.prognosis: Many improve with load management and progressive strengthening, but recovery is often slower than patients expect and a proportion report symptoms years later. Set that expectation early.
misconceptions: Crepitus does not indicate joint damage and is common in painless knees.
Imaging findings correlate poorly with symptoms and rarely change management.
Dynamic valgus is a common treatment target, not a diagnostic criterion.

additionalFindings.text: Quadriceps and gluteal weakness are frequently found
additionalFindings.detail: Whether weakness causes the pain or results from it is not resolved. It remains a reasonable treatment target either way.

managementDetail: Combine hip and knee exercise rather than knee-only programmes.
Adjuncts such as taping or foot orthoses may help some patients short-term.
Reassess with the same functional task each visit so progress is visible.

references: Willy RW, Hoglund LT, Barton CJ, et al. Patellofemoral pain: clinical practice guidelines linked to the ICF. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2019;49(9):CPG1-CPG95.

statistics.source: Accuracy figures not entered. Guidelines advise against relying on individual palpation or compression tests.

evidence.limitations: The diagnosis rests on a clinical pattern rather than a reference standard, so reported test accuracy is difficult to interpret and is not used here.
